The continuity plan provides a framework to ensure the county's essential functions continue when disruptions impact service delivery. Our organization operates under an enterprise-wide continuity plan supported by department-specific plans. You might wonder what continuity planning is, but you probably know more about it than you think.

Weekday mornings, most folks have a morning routine to get ready for the day and then commute to school and work. An example of continuity planning at home may include considerations about what to do if the car doesn't start or if a kid is sick or has to stay home. Anticipating disruptions and having backup plans are very important so that our day-to-day lives can run smoothly without big interruptions.

We aim to do the same for local government, knowing that disruptions in service can impact a lot of people across the community. Over the past year, we've made significant progress in strengthening our ability to deliver critical services under any circumstance. In Phase 1, we appointed 17 continuity liaisons across departments to assist with planning.

Together, we identified essential functions, key personnel, and over 153 vital records. We also established orders of succession for 79 key positions, ensuring leadership continuity. Today, every county department has its own continuity plan.

As we move into Phase 2, our focus shifts to implementation and refinement. We'll conduct quarterly program meetings, provide department-specific training, and test plans through exercises. This will culminate in a county-wide continuity exercise in the next fiscal year.

The continuity program reflects Albemarle County's commitment to resilience and preparedness. By working together across departments, we're building a stronger, more adaptable organization ready to serve our community in any situation. Keeping children safe on their way to and from school is one of Albemarle County's highest priorities.

The school's own speed camera program, which launched on September 3rd, 2024, was developed in response to community concerns about speeding near schools and supported by speed studies conducted on hydraulic roads. These studies identified areas where speeding posed the risk to student safety, particularly near Lambs Lane campus, home to Elkhart High School, Journey Middle School, and Greer Elementary School.

Informed by data and community input, the program focuses on reducing speed and creating a safer environment for everyone. For the first 45 days, drivers who exceeded the speed limit by 10 miles per hour or more in the school zone received warnings instead of citations. This period was designed to educate drivers and give everyone time to adjust for the new enforcement measures.

During this time period, nearly 6,000 warnings were issued to motorists. Full enforcement began in October, and drivers now receive $100 citations if they exceed the speed limit by 10 miles per hour or more when the school zone lights are flashing. This program reflects our focus on safety, accountability, and compliance.

The benefits of this program extend beyond immediate enforcement. By encouraging safer driving behaviors, we're protecting students, families, teachers, and staff. Lower speeds also create a safer environment, ensuring that everyone traveling through these areas feels secure. This initiative wouldn't be possible without our partnership with Elmore County Public Schools.

With proven results from similar programs across Virginia, including a 55% reduction in speed violations within three months, We're confident this program will make a meaningful difference in our community. By working together, we are ensuring that school zones are safer for everyone.
